newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia military "says no to Megawati politics".
newsitem.headline: Indonesia military "says no to Megawati politics".

text.p: Indonesia's military has said opposition figurehead Megawati Sukarnoputri and her followers do not have the right to carry out political activities, Republika newspaper reported on Monday.

The newspaper quoted Lieutenant-General Syarwan Hamid, chief of the military's social and political affairs division, as saying that Megawati's plan to open a headquarters of her faction of the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) was also unacceptable.

Megawati is scheduled to open the new headquarters later on Monday. Police are in control of the PDI's main party office in central Jakarta, which they raided on July 27 to evict Megawati's supporters.

The supporters had taken over the building after Megawati, the daughter of late founding president Sukarno, was ousted from the PDI leadership by a government-backed party faction and replaced by deputy parliamentary speaker Surjadi.
"Basically the government only recognizes Surjadi as chief of the central executive board of the PDI," Hamid was quoted as saying by the newspaper.

The police raid on the party headquarters in July led to riots in which at least five people died and scores of buildings and vehicles were set ablaze. It was the worst violence in Jakarta for more than two decades.
Hamid said the government would not accept political activities carried out by Megawati's supporters including proposing candidates for parliamentary elections scheduled for next year.
"They do not have the legitimacy to carry out those (political activities)," Hamid said.
Indonesia's military is allowed by the constitution to have a major say in internal affairs, including politics.

The military and the government have backed the Surjadi faction of the PDI, which political analysts have said is a move aimed at preventing Megawati from cutting into the ruling Golkar party's vote in the elections.

Analysts have also said the government is afraid Megawati could stand against President Suharto in the 1998 presidential elections. Suharto, who took over from Sukarno in the mid-1960s, has been elected unopposed for six consecutive terms.
He has not said if he will stand for a seventh time but is widely expected to.
